summary:
Ontario stands under Canada's national framework, which carries federal criminal law and federal human-rights protections; the province's own layer is the Ontario Human Rights Code and the policy the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes under it.

The Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that the Code protects people from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. It defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and records that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate of police-recorded hate crimes in 2024, 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, against a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The figures count police-reported incidents only.

On 28 August 2023 Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents must be fully involved and fully aware of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh exceptional circumstances and potential harm to the child. Ontario did not adopt legislation requiring parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names or pronouns at that time.
tangentialFactors:
The dispute over names and pronouns in schools concerns minors and school boards rather than adult visitors, but it is the clearest signal in the sources of the provincial government's posture on trans recognition. The minister's statement was not followed by legislation.

Ontario's hate-crime figure is published as a rate per 100,000 rather than a raw count, so the province's position at the top of the provincial table is not an artefact of its population size.
localsOnly:
Residents can bring discrimination complaints on gender identity and gender expression under the Ontario Human Rights Code in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and union or professional-association membership; the Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy is the official statement of that law.

For residents with children in Ontario schools, the education minister's August 2023 position is that parents must be fully involved and fully aware when a student decides to use a different name or pronoun, with teachers and school boards weighing exceptional circumstances and potential harm; no parental-consent statute was enacted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed do not set out Ontario's requirements for changing the gender marker on provincial documents.

Hate-crime counts are police-recorded and capture only incidents that were reported; reporting levels are shaped by awareness and by community trust in police, so the recorded rate reflects both incidence and willingness to report.

Whether Ontario will legislate parental consent for students under 16 who request a different name or pronoun is unresolved; the minister's 2023 statement was not accompanied by a bill.

A national hate-crime analysis covering gender-identity motivations exists, but its Ontario-level breakdown is not in the sources reviewed.
